overview: The Amorúa are an Indigenous people of the Orinoco region, with communities in Vichada and Casanare and histories of movement across the Colombia-Venezuela border. Their own research emphasizes remembered routes, relationships among communities, food knowledge and self-government. Rural settlements, resguardos and urban neighborhoods are all part of their recent history.

periods.title: Violence and disrupted movement
periods.summary: Researchers connect twentieth-century dispersal with partisan violence in the 1950s and appropriation of land by settlers. Subsequent conflict and commercial pressures brought further changes. These disruptions cannot be reduced to one conquest date.

periods.title: Organizing craft work at Guáripa
periods.summary: Guáripa artisans date a renewed effort to strengthen their work to 2005. They organized gathering and preparation of materials, chose a coordinator and worked to improve the quality and sale of woven goods.

periods.title: Community-led memory research
periods.summary: Between April and November 2013, researchers from six Amorúa communities worked with Etnollano and the Ministry of Culture. They recorded knowledge in maps, drawings, interviews and books, then shared their findings.

periods.title: Documenting food knowledge at La Esmeralda
periods.summary: Interviews and workshops at La Esmeralda documented food preparation, seasonal resources and changes in access to land. This community evidence should not be mistaken for a description of every Amorúa settlement.

periods.title: A collective reparation milestone
periods.summary: Kanalitojo, whose residents include Amorúa, Sikuani and Sáliba people, marked completion of its collective reparation plan. The program addressed particular conflict-related harms and supported community institutions and livelihoods.

items.text: The La Esmeralda study documents a sebucán, called woboto, used to squeeze bitter manioc. It connects the implement with plants gathered for household production. This is evidence of working material knowledge in a living community, not an archaeological object or proof that the Amorúa invented manioc processing.

At La Esmeralda, fishing depended on access to rivers, channels and a lagoon. Residents described lower river levels during the dry season and changes in available catches. Knowledge of water and season helped households obtain food; the account does not establish an unchanging calendar for all Amorúa communities.

Families sold manioc products such as mañoco and casabe in Agua Verde and bought soap, salt and other supplies. To reduce transport costs, one person could carry goods for several households. The documented arrangement shows practical cooperation connecting local food production with river travel and market exchange.

Guáripa artisans describe extracting fibers individually from young moriche leaves, cooking them in water and drying them in shade. They also explain harvesting leaves without felling the palm and allowing plants to recover. Preparing material and sustaining its supply are part of the same craft knowledge.

The Guáripa booklet shows hand-twisted fiber and coiled basketry. Its dye chart associates orange with onoto and brown with algarrobo. The artisans describe using inherited knowledge and experimenting with plants. Their work therefore includes investigation and refinement, rather than simply copying a permanently fixed set of designs.

The group’s account credits Rosa Juana with encouraging women to renew weaving. Organization brought coordination of materials, better-quality work and opportunities to sell beyond nearby towns. The narrative records a particular community’s achievement; it does not suggest that weaving had disappeared among all Amorúa people.

Gobierno Mayor describes homes using palm roofs, timber supports, board walls and earth floors, alongside brick buildings. Hammocks form part of this domestic setting. The account shows several building materials in use; it should not be turned into a rule that every family lives in the same kind of house.

The same Indigenous organization describes a captain who represents the community administratively and politically while consulting traditional authorities. Elders and knowledgeable people remain part of decision-making. This account distinguishes a community leadership role from kingship and does not imply a single centralized government over all Amorúa settlements.

In the study based on 2013 fieldwork, Amorúa speakers recalled making temporary shelters with platanillo leaves during journeys. The authors relate movement to remembered territory and criticize stereotypes that treated mobility as inferiority. Temporary residence was a way of using and knowing a landscape, not evidence of having no homeland.

Community researchers in 2013 drew routes of arrival and discussed their maps with younger and older residents. They also recorded food varieties, fishing and craft practices. Their books and drawings are concrete research products that preserve knowledge while allowing communities to question present problems of territory, education and autonomy.

Casanare’s rural education plan records work with Amorúa and other peoples to develop community educational projects. Elders, authorities and teachers contributed knowledge for study plans addressing territory, history, language and identity. The document reports a shared program; its combined student total cannot be assigned to the Amorúa alone.

A 2012 SENA report records Amorúa and Sikuani participants presenting fiber and natural-dye work at an exchange in Mitú. Demonstrations introduced visitors to moriche bags and baskets, while a forum addressed organization and fair commerce. Craftsmanship also provided a means of exchanging knowledge with other Indigenous makers.

Kanalitojo’s secretary described families fleeing armed groups, some crossing into Venezuela, and losses of territory. The community’s reparation process began in 2015. By July 2024, the responsible agency reported completion of twelve measures, including a cultural hall, agricultural initiatives and recovery of knowledge. This is a specific program’s reported outcome.

ending.text: Amorúa communities continue despite displacement, land pressures and discrimination. Kanalitojo’s 2024 reparation milestone illustrates ongoing collective organization alongside other Indigenous peoples. Completion of that plan does not establish that every harm has been resolved. The map’s 1500 endpoint is not an extinction date or the end of Amorúa history.
